The damage to schools and loss of learning materials have disrupted education for 3,000 children. Floodwaters have also killed or swept away more than 1,700 livestock in Somaliland and Puntland states, compounding previous drought-related livestock losses. 

Inadequate access to WASH facilities and the possible contamination of water sources during the rainy season could worsen current outbreaks of acute watery diarrhoea and cholera. 

Some IDPs in Banadir region and Hirshabelle, Puntland, and Southwest states face secondary displacement after the floods damaged their makeshift shelters. Stagnant floodwaters and damaged roads have made some areas, such as IDP sites in Baidoa town and parts of Dhuusamareeb town, inaccessible. Affected populations need food, shelter, WASH, and NFIs.
([OCHA 03/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-gu-rainy-season-2023-flash-floods-update-no-2-3-april-2023), [UNICEF 04/2023](https://www.unicef.org/somalia/media/3586/file/Baardheere%20Flood%20Emergency%20April%202023.pdf), [Crisis24 25/03/2023](https://crisis24.garda.com/alerts/2023/03/somalia-disruptions-due-to-flooding-ongoing-nationwide-as-of-march-26-update-1))

In March 2023, the Lebanese lira sunk to a new low, losing more than 95% of its value since the socioeconomic crisis started in 2019. 

Around 2.2 million people, including 1.98 million Lebanese (33% of the assessed population), are estimated to be food-insecure and in need of humanitarian assistance in the first quarter of 2023. 

Lebanese residents are facing the most food insecurity in Akkar, Mount Lebanon, and North governorates. The economic crisis has increased the multidimensional poverty rate in 2023 to more than 80%, up from 42% in 2019. The unemployment rate also reached around 30% in 2022 – up from 11% in 2019. The economic crisis is causing Lebanese households to face challenges in accessing food, healthcare, education, and other basic services. 
([The 961 04/04/2023](https://www.the961.com/todays-lebanese-lira-us-dollar-exchange-rate-april-4th-2023/), [VAO 14/03/2023](https://www.voanews.com/a/lebanese-currency-sinks-to-new-low-/7003798.html), [FAO/WFP 19/01/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/economic-crisis-currency-depreciation-and-unprecedented-increase-food-and-non-food-prices-leave-2-million-people-need-assistance-lebanon), [USAID 20/01/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-complex-emergency-fact-sheet-2-fiscal-year-fy-2023-january-20-2023),  [IPC 22/12/2022](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-acute-food-insecurity-situation-september-december-2022-and-projection-january-april-2023-economic-crisis-currency-depreciation-and-unprecedented-increase-food-and-non-food-prices-worsen-lebanon-food-security-situation), [IFRC 03/01/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-2023-ifrc-network-country-plan-mgrlb001), [WB accessed 25/01/2023](https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/lebanon/overview), [ILO 12/05/2022](https://www.ilo.org/beirut/media-centre/news/WCMS_844831/lang--en/index.htm),[UNHCR 16/02/2022](https://data.unhcr.org/en/documents/details/90915))

The aftermath of Tropical Cyclone Freddy in southern Malawi has been devastating, with flooding and landslides affecting an estimated 2.3 million people and leaving more than 670 dead, 500 missing, and over 659,000 displaced. 

The displaced are sheltering in schools, churches, and community centres. Biantyre, Chikwawa, Mulanje, Nsanje, and Phalombe have been the hardest-hit districts. Those affected urgently need WASH services, shelter, food, and NFIs. 
([OCHA 07/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/malawi/malawi-tropical-cyclone-freddy-flash-update-no-12-7-april-2023), [WFP 06/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/malawi/wfp-malawi-cyclone-freddy-response-update-6-april-2023-0800-cat))

Between 5–14 March 2023, over 2,600 refugees from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) fled to Tanzania to escape clashes between the March 23 Movement and the Congolese army in Kivu region. Many, including women, children, and the elderly, sought refuge in Nyarugusu camp in Kigoma, which is already overcrowded as it houses 130,000 refugees, three times its original capacity. More refugees are expected to arrive in Tanzania as a result of this conflict, intensifying the urgent need for essentials such as food, WASH facilities, shelter, and healthcare. ([ECHO 03/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/united-republic-tanzania/tanzania-rwanda-burundi-refugee-influx-democratic-republic-congo-echo-daily-flash-3-april-2023), [The East African 16/03/2023](https://www.theeastafrican.co.ke/tea/news/east-africa/over-2600-drc-refugees-enter-tanzania-4160800), [The Citizen 15/03/2023](https://www.thecitizen.co.tz/tanzania/news/national/tanzania-receives-2-643-refugees-from-dr-congo-4160216))

On April 4 2023, the Taliban banned Afghan women from working for the UN in Afghanistan, a move that has drawn condemnation from the UN SG. The UN has requested its 3,300 Afghan employees, which include 400 women, to refrain from attending work, with limited exceptions for critical tasks. The ban will limit access to critical services and aid for 28.3 million people and make it more difficult for responders to reach the 11.6 million women and girls in need of assistance. This ban comes at a time when 95% of Afghans, including almost all women-led households, are not getting enough food. The ban will decrease household income and increase pressure on male family members as the sole breadwinners while the country is going through an economic crisis. Limiting employment options for women increases the risk of exposure to protection threats.
The ban is the latest in a series of restrictions imposed on Afghan women by the Taliban since the group regained power in August 2021. The UN is reviewing its presence in Afghanistan given the continued violation of women's rights and the significant disruption to its operations. ([UNAMA 11/04/2023](https://unama.unmissions.org/statement-and-update-united-nations-afghanistan), [Reuters 05/04/2023](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/un-staff-eastern-afghan-province-stopped-reporting-work-statement-2023-04-04/), [OCHA 23/01/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-humanitarian-needs-overview-2023-january-2023), [OCHA 15/03/2023](https://news.un.org/en/story/2022/03/1113982), [Afghanaid 03/01/2023](https://www.afghanaid.org.uk/news/what-is-happening-to-women-and-ngos-in-afghanistan-and-what-are-the-key-challenges-facing-the-country-in-2023))

As at 10 April 2023, the number of post-coup IDPs in Kayin state, southeastern Myanmar, was around 116,000. Movement restrictions, conflict, and insecurity have impeded the work of humanitarian responders and constrained the delivery of humanitarian aid, including NFIs and shelter assistance, to affected and displaced people in multiple states and regions, including Kayin state. 

Since 5 April, around 9,200 people fled from Shwe Kokko, a town in Myawaddy township in Kayin state, to Thailand given the escalation of conflict between the ethnic armed organisation Karen National Liberation Army, along with its allies, and the Myanmar military since late March. These refugees were provided shelter in 13 Temporary Safety Areas (TSAs) in Mae Sot and Mae Ramat in Tak province. As at 10 April, around 960 refugees remained in three TSAs with the rest returning to Myanmar. They were provided with food, water, medical care, shelter, and core relief items.

Heavy rains since early March and the passage of Cyclone Yaku have caused flooding and landslides in Peru, especially in the northern coastal area and Lima city. 

As at 6 April, some 241,000 people have been affected and at least 95,000 homes and 275 health centres have been damaged or destroyed. Although the number of Venezuelans affected is unknown, Tumbes, the main entry point for Venezuelans travelling from Ecuador was affected by the floods. Urgent humanitarian needs include access to safe drinking water and the repair of water distribution systems, as there is an increased risk of waterborne diseases and malaria. 63,000 hectares of crops have been affected or lost. Some roads have been damaged, so access to the north is restricted.   
([UNICEF 08/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/peru/unicef-peru-humanitarian-situation-report-no1-reporting-period-1-march-4-april-2023), [Infobae accessed 11/04/2023](https://www.infobae.com/peru/2023/03/09/lluvias-en-vivo-emergencia-por-cliclon-yaku-desborde-de-rios-y-quebradas-en-el-norte-del-pais/))

Over 2,600 confirmed cases of dengue fever, 8,000 suspected cases, and 45 related deaths were reported in Sudan between July 2022 and March 2023, with the healthcare system strained from responding to other infectious diseases, including measles and malaria. The shortage of medical equipment, including blood bags and test kits, with only one laboratory that can confirm vector-borne diseases, is hampering case identification. Since 5 April, around 9,200 people fled from Shwe Kokko, a town in Myawaddy township in Kayin state, to Thailand given the escalation of conflict between the ethnic armed organisation Karen National Liberation Army, along with its allies, and the Myanmar military since late March. These refugees were provided shelter in 13 Temporary Safety Areas (TSAs) in Mae Sot and Mae Ramat in Tak province. As at 10 April, around 960 refugees remained in three TSAs with the rest returning to Myanmar. They were provided with food, water, medical care, shelter, and core relief items.

([UNHCR 11/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/map/myanmar/myanmar-emergency-overview-map-number-people-displaced-feb-2021-and-remain-displaced-10-apr-2023, [Mizzima 11/04/2023](https://www.mizzima.com/article/10000-flee-shwe-kokko-fighting-thailand), [BBC 08/04/2023](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-65210336), [ECHO 07/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/thailand/thailand-myanmar-refugee-influx-tak-province-dg-echo-media-echo-daily-flash-07-april-2023), [The Irrawaddy 07/04/2023](https://www.irrawaddy.com/news/burma/resistance-raids-myanmar-junta-outposts-near-chinese-gambling-hub.html))

On 4 April 2023, Israeli forces raided holy sites in Jerusalem, resulting in the beating up and injuring of hundreds of Palestinian worshippers and highlighting the increase in violence in the West Bank in the month of April. 

The rise in violence is increasing the humanitarian needs of Palestinians, including protection from risks that include threats to life, insecurity, loss of property, and movement restrictions. 
([UN HRC 06/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/israel-un-expert-condemns-brutal-attacks-palestinians-al-aqsa-mosque), [Al Jazeera 02/04/2023](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/4/2/israeli-soldier-kills-palestinian-in-west-bank-as-violence-rises), [UN 05/04/2023](https://press.un.org/en/2023/gapal1451.doc.htm), [OCHA 31/12/2020](https://www.ochaopt.org/sites/default/files/hno_2021.pdf), [OCHA 31/03/2023](https://www.ochaopt.org/poc/14-27-march-2023))

Tropical Cyclone Freddy made two landfalls on 21 February and 4 March 2023, affecting approximately 299,000 people, displacing over 70,000 people, killing 17 people, destroying homes, and causing major damage to public infrastructure. Those displaced are mostly hosted in schools, some of which were already previously affected by Cyclone Cheneso. Those affected are in need of WASH facilities, shelter, food, and NFIs. ([WFP 06/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/madagascar/wfp-madagascar-cyclone-response-update-6-april-2023), [ECHO 15/03/2023](https://reliefweb.int/map/madagascar/madagascar-malawi-mozambique-tropical-cyclone-freddy-dg-echo-daily-map-15032023))

Cyclone Freddy struck Mozambique twice, making landfall on 24 February 2023 and then again on 21 March, affecting 8 out of the 11 provinces in the country. The cyclone affected an estimated 1.1 million people, caused extensive damage to infrastructure, and destroyed 391,000 hectares of cropland, resulting in the loss of livelihoods and 53 lives. As at 10 April, approximately 57,000 individuals out of the 184,000 people displaced by the cyclone still resided in 33 accommodation sites across Inhambane, Niassa, Sofala, Tete, and Zambezia provinces. The cyclone affected women and children the most (respectively 33% and 44% of these groups). Those affected are in urgent need of food, shelter, WASH, health, protection, and NFIs. ([IOM 10/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-floods-tropical-storm-freddy-accommodation-centres-dashboard-10-april-2023), [AP 23/03/2023](https://apnews.com/article/climate-change-cyclone-freddy-malawi-mozambique-3eea4165dbf5ed7b2ee52b0357159a94), [PBS 11/03/2023](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/cyclone-freddy-returns-to-strike-mozambique-for-second-time-since-late-february))

Since the beginning of the Gu rainy season in March 2023, flash and riverine floods have affected over 175,000 people, with 140,000 displaced as at 13 April. Most IDPs are in Baardheere district in the Gedo region of Jubaland state and Baidoa district in the Bay region of Southwest state. 

The flooding has caused livestock losses and damaged roads, schools, health centres, farmlands, and homes, affecting access to food and livelihoods, health, and education. Floodwaters have swept away around 27,500 livestock in the Gedo region of Jubaland state and killed 1,700 livestock in Somaliland and Puntland states, compounding previous drought-related livestock losses. 

Stagnant water and inadequate access to WASH facilities also increase the risk of waterborne diseases such as acute watery diarrhoea and cholera. Since January, around 4,000 suspected cholera cases (over 50% being children) with 15 associated deaths have been reported.

([OCHA 13/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-gu-rainy-season-2023-flash-floods-update-no-3-13-april-2023), [OCHA 03/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-gu-rainy-season-2023-flash-floods-update-no-2-3-april-2023), [WHO 19/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/weekly-choleraawd-situation-report-somalia-epidemiological-week-13-27-march-2-april-2023))

As at 18 April, conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) had resulted in more than 180 fatalities and over 1,800 injuries. In North Darfur, fighting has led to the deaths of at least three aid workers and the wounding of two others. Attacks on humanitarian premises and looting in several areas have led to the suspension of aid operations in most parts of the country. The latest clashes will worsen existing humanitarian needs, as one-third of the population faces Stressed (IPC Phase 2) and Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity, including more than 600,000 children under the age of five who face severe acute malnutrition. Before this conflict, there were already 3.7 million IDPs, and rates of displacement are likely to increase. Shortages of blood, oxygen, vital medicine, and fuel are further straining an already fragile health system. Affected populations require food, water, healthcare, and protection, which would require a humanitarian ceasefire to restart operations. ([Al Jazeera 17/04/2023](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/4/17/more-than-180-people-killed-in-sudan-fighting-un-envoy-to-sudan), [Save the Children 17/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/sudan-armed-groups-loot-medical-supplies-and-aid-save-children), [UN News 16/04/2023](https://news.un.org/en/story/2023/04/1135707), [OCHA 13/04/2023] (https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/sudan-situation-report-13-april-2023-enar))

The security situation continues to deteriorate in Menaka region as a result of clashes between non-state armed groups and attacks against civilians. Non-state armed groups attacking neighbouring communes have led to more than 30,000 people fleeing to Menaka town.

These displaced people are in overcrowded houses or makeshift camps set up on roadsides or outside the town, with an urgent need for drinking water, food, medicine, and shelter assistance.

Since 10 April 2023, the Sahelian branch of the Islamic State has taken control of the locality of Tidermene, one of the main supply routes for Menaka town. This means that humanitarian access to Menaka town is likely to deteriorate.

The extension of the influence area of armed groups in northeastern Mali raises fears of an increase in protection incidents and targeted attacks against certain communities perceived as supporting either the Malian army or other armed groups. ([RFI 11/04/2023](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20230411-mali-le-groupe-%C3%A9tat-islamique-prend-tiderm%C3%A8ne-m%C3%A9naka-en-sursis), [RFI 16/04/2023](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20230415-mali-quelles-cons%C3%A9quences-peut-avoir-la-progression-du-groupe-%C3%A9tat-islamique), [RFI 13/04/2023](https://www.france24.com/fr/afrique/20230413-mali-le-groupe-%C3%A9tat-islamique-au-grand-sahara-aux-portes-de-m%C3%A9naka?utm_term=France24_fr&utm_campaign=nonli&utm_source=twitter&utm_medium=social), [MINUSMA 17/04/2023](https://minusma.unmissions.org/devant-le-conseil-de-s%C3%A9curit%C3%A9-le-chef-de-la-minusma-alerte-sur-les-besoins-des-civils-%C3%A0-m%C3%A9naka), [TV5 Monde 13/04/2023](https://information.tv5monde.com/afrique/mali-l-ei-en-pleine-progression-prend-une-localite-cle-de-la-region-de-menaka-495150))

Overall, 10.7 million people in Ukraine need mine action assistance in 2023. The total estimated area contaminated with explosive ordnance because of the conflict is around 174,000km2. Conflict and mine contamination means that around 25% of agricultural land is not accessible. The situation for Afghan refugees in Iran is becoming increasingly difficult. Since January 2023, over 250,000 refugees returned to Afghanistan from Iran, at least half of them facing some form of coercion. Displaced Afghan people face protection risks, including family separation, violence, and persecution. The situation is particularly unpredictable for undocumented people, who have limited access to services. The process of renewing documentation for refugees has also become more complicated, putting documented refugees at risk of becoming undocumented. Access to education has been impeded by the lack of documentation, affordability, and child labour. The situation is compounded by the political and economic situation in Iran, where social unrest and inflation (64% in March 2023) are making it difficult for refugees to meet their basic needs. Limited livelihood opportunities and restricted access to employment have lowered purchasing power and increased protection risks from negative coping strategies. Afghan refugees in Iran face discrimination and growing resentment caused by economic pressure and perceived competition for jobs. Despite Iran's history of being inclusive to refugees, recent reports show the mistreatment towards Afghan refugees by both government officials and civilians, including physical abuse and wrongful detention. ([IOM 19/04/2023](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/movement-and-out-afghanistan-snapshot-1-31-mar-2023?close=true), [UNHCR 09/03/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/pakistan/afghanistan-situation-regional-refugee-response-plan-rrp-january-december-2023), [EU 11/01/2023](https://euaa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/publications/2023-01/2023_01_COI_Report_Iran_Afghans_Refugees_EN.pdf), [The Khaama Press 27/03/2023](https://www.khaama.com/acting-minister-of-refugees-iranian-ambassador-discuss-afghan-refugees-problems-in-kabul/#:~:text=There%20are%20many%20different%20ways,their%20freedom%20of%20movement%2C%20forced), [Iran International 02/04/2023](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202304024947))

Around 960,000 IDPs are estimated to live in Myanmar's Magway and Sagaing regions. Temperatures higher than usual have exposed these IDPs (especially the elderly and young) to health risks, including heatstroke and dehydration. Many of them do not have adequate shelter and access to sufficient water. Several villages have been targeted in the post-coup conflict, which has hindered displaced people’s access to existing water sources. IDPs also need rehydration salts.

([UNHCR 24/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/map/myanmar/myanmar-unhcr-displacement-overview-24-apr-2023), [The Irrawaddy 21/04/2023](https://www.irrawaddy.com/news/burma/extreme-heat-hammers-myanmars-displaced-civilians.html))

Between 16–30 April, more than 23,600 displaced people crossed from Sudan to South Sudan, fleeing the conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that erupted in Sudan on 15 April. The number of arrivals is likely higher because they are not being registered at the border and will continue to increase as the crisis unfolds. Most of the arrivals are South Sudanese, while the rest are Eritrean, Kenyan, Somali, Sudanese, and Ugandan. The main points of entry are in Renk, Upper Nile and Aweil North, Northern Bahr el Ghazal. The Government and international actors are mobilising a response effort as humanitarian needs are likely to increase, including the need for food, water, shelter, and onward transportation. There are 1.1 million refugees in Sudan, including over 800,000 South Sudanese, with humanitarian organisations likely to assist about 125,000 of them to return to South Sudan. ([OCHA 25/05/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-snapshot-april-2023)), ([Reuters 24/04/2023](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/south-sudan-receives-about-10000-refugees-fleeing-sudan-fighting-2023-04-24/)), ([AA 25/04/2023](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/africa/south-sudan-receives-thousands-fleeing-from-sudan-conflict/2880550)), ([TVP 25/04/2023](https://tvpworld.com/69434318/hundreds-of-thousands-may-flee-sudan-fighting-un-refugee-agency)), ([UNHCR 25/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/unhcr-mobilizes-help-people-fleeing-sudan-neighbouring-countries)), ([UNHCR accessed 26/04/2023](https://data2.unhcr.org/en/country/sdn))

On 18 April 2023, the Iraqi Government closed the Jeddah 5 IDP camp in Ninewa Governorate, forcing the 342 families (1,566 residents, almost two thirds of whom are children) to leave the camp. The closure is part of a government plan that began in 2019 to close all IDP camps in the country. Jeddah 5 was one of the last two remaining IDP camps in areas under the control of the Iraqi Federal Government.

Both the residents and humanitarian responders in the camp were only notified two days in advance. In previous camp closures, the majority of IDPs returned to their homes, but almost half live in inadequate conditions.

There are currently around 1.2 million people internally displaced in Iraq, with the vast majority living in host communities in Dahuk, Erbil, Kirkuk, Ninewa, and Sulaymaniyah governorates. 

IDPs' most urgent needs include healthcare, food, livelihoods, shelter, and protection. ([iDMC 19/05/2022](https://www.internal-displacement.org/countries/iraq), [UN Iraq 19/04/2023](https://iraq.un.org/en/228270-statement-office-humanitarian-coordinator-iraq-closure-jeddah-5-camp), [RUDAW 19/04/2023](https://www.rudaw.net/english/middleeast/iraq/190420235), ([DTM accessed 22/03/2023](http://iraqdtm.iom.int/Dashboard))

Despite the permanent cessation of hostilities signed in November 2022, the two-year conflict in northern Ethiopia has had a significant impact on education. Schools are expected to reopen in May 2023, but over 2.3 million children in northern Ethiopia are still unable to attend school because of the conflict, and 22,500 teachers have not been paid for over two years. In Tigray, most schools have been damaged or destroyed, and all public schools are closed. Children who are unable to attend school are exposed to the risk of child marriage, labour, exploitation, and sexual violence. There is an urgent need to provide assistance in the education sector and address protection concerns. ([Save the Children 12/04/2023](https://reliefweb.int/report/ethiopia/more-23-million-children-out-school-northern-ethiopia-despite-peace-agreement)), ([Mereja 21/04/2023](https://mereja.com/index/442415))

An estimated 20,000 Chadians and Sudanese have crossed to Chad since 15 April 2023, while another 100,000 are likely to arrive mostly from Nyala and El Geneina towns. As at 22 April, the violence had produced as many as 37,000 IDPs in Nyala and 17,000 in North Darfur. The new arrivals are staying in Ouaddai and Sila provinces in Chad and need food, water, and shelter. ([IOM 25/04/2023](https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/situation_reports/file/iom_sudan_situation-update_25_april_2023.pdf)), [(Al Jazeera 26/04/2023](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/4/26/humanitarian-fears-as-thousands-of-sudanese-flee-to-chad-on-foot))
